hypothesis: Unmodified scaffold RandomForest establishes the starting RMSE for BEV.
observation: RMSE 0.013345 in 7.1s on 2017 Chevy Bolt data. Training finishes well under the 10-minute budget.
reasoning: With 8-9 minutes of budget unused, there is ample room to scale the model and add features. BEV energy is heavy-tailed (regen negatives), so tree-based non-parametric models should handle the distribution out of the box.

hypothesis: HGBR at defaults will beat RF(n=20, d=10) on BEV because GBMs handle heavy-tailed asymmetric targets better and are not capped at max_depth=10.
observation: RMSE 0.013347 in 4.6s - essentially tied with RF baseline (+0.015% worse, numerical noise). HGBR is ~35% faster to train, so there is headroom for more boosting iterations.
reasoning: HGBR defaults (max_iter=100) are under-parameterized relative to the baseline RF's effective capacity. The family swap alone does nothing - the value will come from scaling HGBR's iterations. Revert and retry with more capacity.

hypothesis: 10x more trees reduces forest variance and should cut RMSE meaningfully. At baseline's 7.1s, 200 trees should fit well within the 10-min budget.
observation: RMSE 0.013341 (-0.03%) in 23.5s. Improvement is tiny - 10x trees barely moved the needle. Linear scaling of train time confirms trees, not depth, is the bottleneck.
reasoning: Variance reduction from more trees has diminishing returns once n>=100. The next lever is bias: max_depth=10 likely caps expressivity with only 3 input features, and min_samples_split=10 limits leaf resolution. Try lifting depth/leaf constraints next.

hypothesis: Depth cap of 10 was limiting fit quality; uncapping lets trees express interaction structure and cut RMSE.
observation: RMSE 0.013964 (+4.7%) in 49.5s - clear overfit. Trees memorize the training distribution, including regen tail outliers that don't generalize.
reasoning: With only 3 input features and 160k+ rows, unlimited depth has no regularization so it memorizes noise. The BEV target has heavy regen tails that are per-sample outliers, not learnable structure. Moderate depth lift with leaf regularization is the right direction, not free depth.

hypothesis: Explicit v^2 gives trees a kinetic-energy nonlinearity without burning depth on approximation, should lower RMSE.
observation: RMSE 0.013341 - exactly tied with best (6-decimal match). Training 30.8s. Zero gain from the added feature.
reasoning: Trees partition speed_mph freely and can capture any monotone-in-v^2 split via speed_mph directly; v^2 adds no information a depth-10 forest cannot already express. Monotone transforms are redundant for trees. Future feature engineering should focus on INTERACTIONS (speed*grade, grade*miles) not monotone transforms of existing features.

description: add prev_speed_mph (previous-link speed, per-journey shift, fillna to self for first link)
hypothesis: Prior-link speed gives the model the vehicle's entry kinetic state, which determines how much of the current link's energy is accel/decel vs cruise. Particularly important for BEV where regen recovery on decel and accel cost are first-order terms.
observation: RMSE 0.009155 (-31.4%) in 29.1s. Massive gain from a single feature. This is the largest single-change improvement likely available.
reasoning: Link-independent features (speed, grade, miles) cannot distinguish a 30mph cruise from a 60->30 deceleration - same average speed, very different energy. Previous-link speed encodes the accel/decel direction and magnitude. This feature is available at inference (domain.md), so the win is real. Expect similar gains from other prev-link features (prev_grade, prev_miles, speed_delta).

hypothesis: Previous-link grade gives complementary state info (coasting from descent vs laboring from climb) that prev_speed alone does not encode.
observation: RMSE 0.009144 (-0.12%) in 35.8s. Small but real gain - much smaller than prev_speed.
reasoning: Prev_grade adds an independent dimension to vehicle-entry state but most of the information was already captured by prev_speed (since speed responds to grade). Marginal but worth keeping. Train time still well under budget.

hypothesis: Explicit accel proxy lets trees split on a single feature instead of needing paired splits on speed + prev_speed, freeing depth budget for other interactions.
observation: RMSE 0.008267 (-9.6%) in 43.3s. Much larger than expected - this contradicts the exp4 hypothesis that tree-internal nonlinearities are always redundant.
reasoning: Key insight: differences between features (speed_delta) are NOT monotone transforms and are NOT cheap for depth-capped trees to express. Explicit differences are worth trying even when the component features are already present. Monotone transforms (v^2) are redundant; differences/interactions generally are NOT. This is a cross-cutting lesson.

hypothesis: Same reasoning as speed_delta - explicit grade change helps depth-capped trees capture slope-change signal cheaply.
observation: RMSE 0.008258 (-0.11%) in 50.7s. Tiny but strictly better.
reasoning: Grade changes have much smaller dynamic range than speed changes in this data, so the signal is weaker. Still confirms the 'explicit differences are not redundant' pattern from exp7.

hypothesis: Multiplicative power term captures signed energy rate on climb/descent at given speed, not easily derived by depth-10 trees from the marginals.
observation: RMSE 0.008247 (-0.13%) in 60.6s. Marginal gain - interaction adds less than speed_delta did.
reasoning: With 8 features and depth 10, each new correlated feature gives diminishing returns. The RF is plateauing. Time to try a different model family (gradient boosting) rather than more feature engineering.

hypothesis: With 8 features now (including key prev-link + interaction signals), boosting's sequential residual fit should outperform bagged trees. HGBR at defaults was tied at 3 features (exp1); at 8 features the picture should flip.
observation: RMSE 0.008088 (-1.93%) in 6.5s. HGBR defaults now clearly beats the tuned RF, AND trains 10x faster. Massive training-time headroom for HP scaling.
reasoning: Boosting's bias reduction (sequential error-targeting) scales better with feature count than bagging's variance reduction. The exp1 tie at 3 features was a feature-count artifact. Now HGBR has room to grow: max_iter up from 100 to 1000+ easily within budget. Cross-cutting: family comparisons should be done with a competitive feature set, not just the baseline 3.

hypothesis: Default max_iter=100 is under-capacity; bumping to 1000 gives more boosting rounds within the 6.5s train time.
observation: RMSE 0.008088 (identical to default) in 6.3s (actually slightly faster). HGBR's early_stopping='auto' (enabled for n>=10k samples) capped iterations well before 1000. max_iter alone is a no-op under auto early stopping.
reasoning: Cross-cutting lesson: when tuning HGBR, max_iter is coupled with early_stopping. To actually use more iterations, either disable early_stopping OR lower learning_rate (so early stopping delay increases). Try lower LR next.

hypothesis: Smaller steps give smoother residual fit, typically better generalization.
observation: RMSE 0.008137 (+0.6%) in 6.9s. Slightly under-fit - lower LR without compensating max_iter means less total progress.
reasoning: LR reduction must be paired with more iterations. Single-knob LR tuning fails when max_iter is the binding constraint.

hypothesis: Default 31 leaves (~depth 5) is shallow for an 8-feature interaction surface. 127 leaves (~depth 7) give more expressivity per boosting round.
observation: RMSE 0.008015 (-0.9%) in 6.7s. Clear improvement - per-round tree depth was the binding constraint.
reasoning: HGBR's bias/capacity knob is leaf count, not iter count (since early stopping gates iter). Keep scanning leaves; try 255 next.

hypothesis: More leaves per tree keeps adding expressivity.
observation: RMSE 0.008011 (-0.05%) in 8.0s. Saturated - leaf count alone is a spent lever.
reasoning: Returns have decayed. The remaining HGBR slack is in max_iter x early_stopping x learning_rate - all three coupled. Try the bundled recipe: unbounded boosting with finer LR.

hypothesis: Smaller LR needs more iters; paired together they let early stopping choose a longer, finer-grained fit.
observation: RMSE 0.008012 in 9.8s - essentially tied with default LR at max_leaf_nodes=255. Added 2 HPs for no gain.
reasoning: HGBR's auto early stopping finds near-optimal iter-count under default LR too; LR schedule adjustments don't unlock more signal once leaves are big enough. HGBR is saturated on tabular. Switch family to LGBM or XGB, or go back to features.

hypothesis: LGBM typically edges out sklearn's HGBR on tabular at same HP budget.
observation: RMSE 0.008061 in 5.3s - worse. LGBM's default num_leaves=31 matches HGBR's default leaves=31, but we tuned HGBR to 255 so this is an unfair comparison.
reasoning: Family comparisons must be at matched capacity. Retry LGBM with num_leaves=255 to match the HGBR best.

description: switch to LGBM with num_leaves=255 (matched capacity)
hypothesis: At matched tree capacity, LGBM's implementation should equal or edge HGBR.
observation: RMSE 0.008007 (-0.05%) in 6.4s. Marginal improvement. LGBM confirms family choice isn't the main lever right now.
reasoning: LGBM gives us more HP knobs (n_estimators without auto-early-stopping gate, min_child_samples, feature_fraction). Unlike HGBR, n_estimators is a real lever for LGBM - try scaling it.

hypothesis: LGBM has no built-in early stopping, so raising n_estimators should actually use the extra capacity.
observation: RMSE 0.008061 (+0.7%) in 12.8s. 500 boosting rounds at num_leaves=255 overfits - no implicit regularization to stop it.
reasoning: Wide trees (leaves=255) + long boosting (500 iters) is an overfit combo. LGBM defaults are calibrated together; breaking one side without compensating regularization hurts. Pivot back to features - model tuning is near saturation.

hypothesis: Gravity-work-on-link is the physically-primary energy term for BEV; explicit product lets trees latch onto it with single splits.
observation: RMSE 0.008004 (-0.04%) in 6.5s. Tiny gain - at num_leaves=255 the interaction was mostly already captured internally.
reasoning: With wide trees (255 leaves) interactions are cheaper to learn so explicit products help less than they did with narrow trees. Still worth keeping - physics-motivated and trains fast.

hypothesis: Prior link distance signals how long the vehicle was in its entering state - short prev links = transient, long prev links = cruising steady-state.
observation: RMSE 0.007502 (-6.3%) in 6.9s. Big gain - prev_miles is the second-most-valuable prev-link feature after prev_speed.
reasoning: Prev_miles combined with prev_speed informs traffic history and time-at-speed - the model can infer 'was this a long cruise that just ended?' vs 'is the vehicle still spinning down from a brief burst?'. Cross-cutting: ALL prev_* lag features appear to carry independent signal on this partition.

hypothesis: Deeper speed history captures trajectory trend (accel/decel phase vs just started braking) that single-step prev_speed misses.
observation: RMSE 0.007056 (-6.0%) in 7.2s. Big gain - 2-step history is materially better than 1-step. Deeper history likely also helps.
reasoning: Trajectory-shape info (is the car still slowing, or already coasting?) requires >1 prior step. prev_speed + prev2_speed sketches the 3-point speed trajectory. Try prev3, prev4, prev5 next.

hypothesis: Extend speed history window further for trajectory shape.
observation: RMSE 0.007050 (-0.08%) in 7.9s. Tiny improvement - history saturating at step 3.
reasoning: 2-link history captured most of the trajectory-shape signal; step 3 adds little. Probably not worth continuing to prev4/5.
